recession.n: In news and economics, a recession is a period when a country's output shrinks, traditionally for two quarters in a row. Speakers usually say the economy is in recession or slipped into recession, often with no article, while a recession (countable) refers to a particular episode, such as the 2008 recession. It is milder than a depression, which is deeper and lasts longer, and more technical than slump or downturn. Common verbs: enter, emerge from, avoid, trigger.
x: Many shops stayed closed long after the last recession ended.
Economists warned that rising interest rates could push the country into recession.

competitive.n: Two senses share this adjective. Describing a person, it means eager to win, and it can be a compliment or a gentle criticism: she is very competitive. Describing prices, salaries, products or markets, it means good enough to succeed against rivals: competitive rates, a highly competitive industry. Someone who takes part in a contest is a competitor, not a competitive. The adverb is competitively, mostly seen in competitively priced.
x: The shop offers competitive prices on all its winter clothing.
My brother gets competitive whenever we play cards, even for fun.

dress up.n: Dress up covers three ideas: wearing smart or formal clothes (we dressed up for the wedding), wearing a costume (dress up as a pirate), and making something look better than it really is (dress up the facts). It is separable with any object: dress the children up or dress up the children. A pronoun must sit in the middle, so say dress them up, never dress up them. Its opposite is dress down, meaning to wear casual clothes.
x: You do not need to dress up for dinner; the restaurant is quite relaxed.
Every Halloween my sister likes to dress up as a different film character.

confine.n: To confine is to keep something inside limits, and the usual pattern is the passive with to: the fire was confined to the top floor. You can also confine yourself to a topic or confine a discussion to key issues. The preposition is the common trap: learners write confined on or at, but it is to for limits and in for a place, as in confined in a small cell. Its root is Latin finis, a boundary, the same source as finish and final. It is more formal than limit.
x: Please confine your answers to the questions on the exam paper.
The outbreak was confined to a single village thanks to quick action.

ethic.n: On its own, the singular ethic is rare and almost always appears in work ethic, a belief that hard work is valuable. For moral principles in general, English prefers the plural ethics, which can take a singular or plural verb: medical ethics is a difficult subject. So the ethic of a company usually becomes the company's ethics or values. The related adjectives are ethical and unethical.
x: Her strong work ethic earned her a promotion within a year.
The company was criticised for ignoring basic business ethics.

contaminate.n: Contaminate means to make something impure or unsafe by adding something harmful, such as chemicals, bacteria or radiation. Its objects are typically water, food, soil, air or a crime scene, and it often takes with or by: the well was contaminated with lead. It sounds more technical than dirty and is narrower than pollute, which is often used for the wider environment. The noun is contamination. Think of con- as together: a harmful thing gets mixed in with something clean.
x: Raw chicken can contaminate other foods if they share the same cutting board.
Oil from the damaged tanker contaminated several kilometres of coastline.

domestication.n: Domestication is the long process by which people breed animals or cultivate plants until they become useful and different from their wild ancestors. It is uncountable, usually followed by of: the domestication of the horse. It is not the same as taming one animal, which can happen in a single lifetime, whereas domestication changes a whole species over many generations. The verb is domesticate; the adjective domestic also means of the home or of one's own country.
x: Scientists still debate when the domestication of the horse first began.
Early farming societies relied heavily on the domestication of cattle and sheep.

forerunner.n: A forerunner is something or someone that came before and prepared the way for a later, better-known thing. It is nearly always followed by of: the radio was a forerunner of television. Precursor is a near synonym that sounds more scientific, whereas forerunner suits history and general writing. Simply being older is not enough; the earlier thing must have influenced what came after. Memory tip: a fore-runner runs ahead of the main group, like a scout.
x: The abacus is often described as a forerunner of the modern calculator.
This small local festival was the forerunner of the city's famous annual carnival.

germinate.n: Germinate describes the moment a seed begins to grow and sends out its first shoot. It is usually intransitive: the beans germinated after a week. Gardeners can also germinate seeds, but that is less common. In writing, an idea can germinate in someone's mind, a slightly literary use. Sprout is the everyday cousin and can describe growth after that first stage. Memory tip: a germ is a beginning, and to germinate is to begin.
x: The seeds will germinate faster if you keep the soil warm and damp.
The idea for the novel began to germinate during a long train journey.

get over.n: Get over means to recover from something upsetting or unpleasant, such as an illness, a shock, a loss or a disappointment. Since it needs an object, you get over the flu or get over a breakup, not simply get over. It also works for physical obstacles (get over a wall) and in the exclamation I cannot get over it, which expresses surprise. Get through is different: it stresses surviving a hard period, not feeling better afterwards.
x: She still cannot get over the shock of losing her job.
It took him months to get over his disappointment at missing the final.

grievance.n: A grievance is a feeling or a formal complaint that you have been treated unfairly, especially at work. Typical verbs are raise, file, air and settle, and the preposition is against a person or about an issue: he has a real grievance against his manager. It is heavier than complaint, because it suggests lasting resentment or an official procedure. Related: aggrieved, the adjective for someone who feels wronged.
x: The union helped her file a grievance about unpaid overtime.
He held a long-standing grievance against the neighbour who cut down his tree.

keep me posted.n: The pattern is keep someone posted on or about something, and it works with other pronouns too: I will keep you posted, keep us posted. It is a friendly, informal way to ask for updates as things develop. It suits friends, family and colleagues you know well, and is too casual for a formal letter, where please inform me of any developments is safer. A close alternative is let me know how it goes.
x: Good luck with your interview tomorrow, and keep me posted on how it goes.
Please keep me posted about the flight so I can pick you up on time.

nutrition.n: Nutrition is how the body receives the food it needs, and also the science that studies it. It is uncountable: good nutrition, never a nutrition. When you talk about the useful substances in one product, nutritional value or nutrients is more precise. A person who advises on this is a nutritionist, and the adjective is nutritional. Diet describes what you usually eat, while nutrition describes whether that food actually supports health and growth.
x: The school offers lessons on nutrition to help students choose healthier meals.
Poor nutrition during pregnancy can affect a baby's long-term health.

organic.n: On food labels, organic means produced without artificial chemicals, and in many countries the label is legally controlled, which makes it stronger than the vague natural. Typical partners: organic farming, organic vegetables, organic cotton. In science it means related to living things, as in organic matter or organic chemistry. In business, organic growth means expansion from a firm's own activities, not from buying other companies. Organic does not automatically mean healthy.
x: We buy organic eggs from a farm that is only ten miles away.
The company aims for organic growth rather than buying smaller competitors.

plateau.n: As a verb, plateau (pronounced plæˈtoʊ, stress on the second syllable) means to stop rising or falling and stay at a steady level: sales plateaued at ten thousand units. Common patterns are plateau at a figure and reach a plateau. In graph descriptions it is a neat alternative to level off, the more everyday phrase. The noun also means a high, flat area of land and, in learning or training, a stage where progress stalls. The word comes from French, where plateau first meant a flat tray or board.
x: Unemployment fell sharply for two years and then plateaued.
My running speed plateaued after a month, so I changed my training plan.

prosperity.n: Prosperity means success and wealth, and it is mostly applied to countries, regions or communities: economic prosperity, a period of prosperity. For a single person, wealth or being well off sounds more natural. It is uncountable. The verb is prosper, the adjective prosperous. A fixed pairing in speeches and writing is peace and prosperity.
x: The new railway brought prosperity to a region that had been poor for decades.
Leaders argued that peace and prosperity depend on fair trade.

upon request.n: A formal phrase meaning if someone asks for it, common on notices, websites and business letters. It collocates with available, provided, sent and free of charge: brochures are available upon request. In ordinary speech and informal writing on request is actually more common, and the meaning is identical; upon only adds formality. It follows a passive verb or adjective, so avoid forms like at request or upon requesting.
x: A full list of ingredients is provided upon request.
Large-print versions of the menu are available upon request at the front desk.

warranty.n: A warranty is a written promise from a maker or seller to repair or replace a product if it fails within a set period. Typical phrases: under warranty, a two-year warranty, extended warranty, void the warranty. It mainly covers faults, not accidents or misuse. Guarantee is very close and more common in speech; warranty is the standard term for cars and electronics. The verb warrant exists but has a different meaning, to justify.
x: The washing machine broke down, but luckily it was still under warranty.
Read the warranty carefully because it does not cover accidental damage.

workforce.n: Workforce means all the people who work for a company, an industry or a country. It is written as one word, and British English allows a singular or plural verb: the workforce is growing, or the workforce are unhappy. Typical partners are skilled workforce, ageing workforce and enter the workforce. It is broader than staff, which usually means the employees of one organisation, and it counts people as a group, not as individuals.
x: The factory laid off a tenth of its workforce during the downturn.
A well-trained workforce is the main reason investors choose this city.

accent.n: An accent is the way someone pronounces words, revealing the region, country or social group they come from. Use it with have: she has a strong Scottish accent. A dialect differs in vocabulary and grammar as well, whereas an accent is about sound only. Many learners say they want to lose their accent, but a better goal is to be clear and easy to understand. Accent can also mean a mark over a letter, as in café, or the stress on a syllable.
x: I could tell from her accent that she grew up in northern England.
Many fluent speakers keep a slight accent from their first language.

assist.n: Assist is a formal verb meaning help, found in writing about work, medicine and customer service. The usual patterns are assist someone with something and assist someone in doing something; assist someone to do something also occurs in formal writing. In casual conversation help sounds more natural. The noun assistance is uncountable, while assistant names the person. Memory tip: it comes from Latin for standing by, so to assist is to stand next to someone.
x: Two nurses will assist the doctor during the operation.
The staff are happy to assist visitors with their luggage.

captivity.n: Captivity is the state of being kept somewhere and not allowed to leave. It is most common for animals in zoos or cages (bred in captivity, born in captivity) and also describes people held prisoner. It is uncountable and takes in, not at. The opposite is in the wild. A captive is the one held. Memory tip: it shares a root with capture, so captivity is what follows being captured.
x: The condor was bred in captivity and then released into the mountains.
After months in captivity, the hostages were finally set free.

collaboratively.n: An adverb meaning by working with others toward a shared result: write, design, develop or solve something collaboratively. It sounds more formal than together and suggests that everyone contributes ideas, not just labour. A frequent error is dropping the adverb ending, as in they worked collaborative; after a verb you need collaboratively. Cooperatively is not identical: it stresses being helpful and not blocking others, while collaboratively stresses creating something jointly.
x: Students in the class learn to solve problems collaboratively.
The software was designed collaboratively by engineers in three countries.

developmental.n: Developmental is the adjective for how a person or thing grows and changes, usually in childhood, and it normally comes before a noun: developmental stage, developmental delay, developmental psychology. Do not mix it up with developing, which describes something still growing, as in a developing country, or with development, the noun. It appears often in education, health and science texts and rarely in casual talk.
x: The nurse checked whether the baby had reached the usual developmental stages.
Developmental problems are easier to treat when they are found early.
